### A micro-intervention for mindful online shopping

Capstone project documentation

Tanya Singh · April 2026


--- 

## The Problem

The average American throws away 37 kilograms of clothing per year.

[Source](https://earth.org/statistics-about-fast-fashion-waste/)

Our closets overflow with clothes we bought on impulse, wore once or twice, and eventually grew bored of. We often don't recognize this cycle, and the easier thing to do is to clear a little space for more, get rid of the old, and repeat it all over again.

This project explores how to introduce a moment of genuine reflection right at the point of purchase, not to block or guilt people, but to help them make decisions they'll actually feel good about.


---

## Background & Rationale

Growing up, I was influenced by my mum and grandmum to make and upcycle my clothes. But I also grew up extremely online. Around 18, I was determined to achieve an amorphous aspirational identity I had created in my head through the content I consumed, and I went through a phase of buying and trying on endless styles.

Things did change a few years later, right around the time the pandemic hit. I was stuck in my messy room and had to confront just how many clothes I had accumulated that I no longer liked. In hindsight, it was very much a symptom of online microtrends and fast fashion.

I ended up upcycling what I could, parting with the rest, and feeling immense relief. Now, as a student who moves frequently, doesn't have a ton of money or space, I avoid fast fashion and have rediscovered my love for preloved and handmade items.

I broke out of that cycle eventually, and admittedly only quite recently. But I know so many people are still stuck in it, especially those aged 18–25, who are in a phase of self-discovery that naturally involves trial and error with clothing and personal style.

Because of my experiences and passions + where the fast fashion industry is headed, I committed to exploring/researching more and building something in this space.

### Primary Research
#### Online Probes 

Working from the insights I gathered from secondary research, I posted probes on two active subreddits (r/anticonsumption and r/sustainableshopping), communities filled with people who have a history of impulse shopping but are committed to breaking the cycle.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
**![328](data:image/png;base64,)
![326](data:image/png;base64,)**

#### Interviews

Based on Reddit responses, I developed an interview protocol and conducted 9 in-depth interviews with participants from these communities and from my personal network.

Interview questions included:

- Where do you typically discover new clothes? (TikTok, friends, stores, influencers?)

- Tell me about the last time you saw clothing online and immediately felt like you needed it.

- When you have items sitting in a cart, what does that feel like? Is it stressful, exciting, or do you just forget about them?

- Can you think of something you bought recently that you were excited about, but now it just sits in your closet? What went wrong?

I deliberately let conversations meander in different directions, hoping to get insights beyond what the Reddit responses revealed. Largely, participants echoed similar views, but the depth of the conversation highlighted important nuances.

#### Affinity Mapping

I synthesized all responses into an affinity map to identify recurring themes. The major themes that emerged were:
  
- Tired of buying poor-quality clothes

- Owning too many unworn clothes

- Delayed purchases and abandoned carts

- The pervasive role of social media influence

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

### Key Insights

The research revealed that the aftermath of the trial-and-error cycle of buying clothes weighs on people, yet they fall into the same patterns. Participants recognized that they resort to impulse buys for mood alleviation, distraction, or simply to have something to look forward to.


> **Perhaps the most important finding was that many people voluntarily delay their purchase at the cart stage.** This natural pause happens for several reasons:
  
- To remove items they're second-guessing

- To ponder whether they really want everything

- To add more items (often prompted by recommended products)

- To close the tab entirely and get busy with something else, after which they either forget about the cart or think about it long enough to return and buy

  
This was the main design opportunity that I identified. People are already breaking out of autopilot at the cart. They're already thinking. I figured, why not emphasize the pause that already takes place at the cart and meet people where they are?

## Competitive Landscape

Before diving into design, I surveyed existing products and interventions designed to prompt reflection at the point of purchase.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

### The Impulse Judge

A web extension with a more playful approach. It surfaces humorous "roasts" that the user is forced to type out (exactly as written) before proceeding to checkout. It only appears at checkout, which is an effective trigger point. However, the layout and visual design are rough, and the 'roast' approach may wear thin over time. I was able to test this particular extension out with past interviewees as well, and they largely shared the same views.

### Think Twice, Buy Once

A mobile app that encourages users to wait a day or two before making a purchase. It features a cleaner layout and tracks money saved. However, it has no pop-up or contextual intervention. Users must manually enter the items they want to buy, adding friction to a process meant to reduce friction-related impulsivity. The app operates entirely outside the shopping context.

### Opportunity Gap

> Neither product combines the strengths of both: contextual, in-the-moment intervention (like The Impulse Judge) with a thoughtful, non-judgmental, well-designed experience (aspired to by Think Twice). Neither uses structured reflection frameworks nor allows users to customize what they reflect on. This is the space Sift aims to fill.

## Ideation & Concept

### The Idea
Design a micro-intervention that takes place right at the cart, at the moment someone is about to check out. Spark a moment of genuine reflection that might deter impulse purchases of clothing or lead to more satisfactory purchases. A win-win.

![[Pasted image 20260417210648.png]]

### Why the Cart?
The impulse purchase pipeline typically starts much earlier, scrolling on social media, seeing an influencer, or encountering a targeted ad. So why intervene at the cart instead of earlier on?

The cart is where people already pause, and after brainstorming where to intervene, this seemed like the most logical approach. Interrupting any other activity would only lead people to disable or delete the 'intervention' altogether. At the cart, an extra layer of structured reflection is added rather than interrupting anything.

### Three Pillars of Reflection
The intervention is structured around three pillars, based on interview responses and analyzing all the data from every research phase, three lenses through which to evaluate a potential purchase:

- **Money:** Can I actually afford this right now? What am I giving up to buy it?

- **Space:** Do I have room for this? Where will it live? What has to move?

- **Need:** Do I genuinely need this, or is it a want? Will I actually use it?

Participants consistently described their regrets as wasted money, overflowing spaces, and items they never actually wore.

---

## Testing the Concept (Physical Card Prototypes)

To test this gap and my insights, I made physical cards and small packets and distributed them to people. This was the only way that seemed feasible to test my idea because it was an unobtrusive way to shop. Participants could take it with them and do the activity whenever they shopped online, so it would be used in context rather than me simulating the experience. I wanted the stakes to be real.
  
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

I knew responses would be few and far between, so I distributed about 70 of these and heard back from 7 people. I collected responses, which helped me strengthen my idea, refine the tone and content design, and consider brand and visual design as well.

![[Screenshot 2026-04-17 at 8.58.19 PM.png]]


---

## The Intervention — Sift

Sift is a Chrome extension that introduces a moment of structured reflection at the checkout transition point on clothing websites. It uses a playing-card metaphor (borrowed directly from my physical testing kit) and prompt cards that feel tactile and fun, rather than highly sanitized modals.

### Design Principles I established early on:

- Sift should feel like a thoughtful friend checking in, never a gatekeeper or a guilt trip.

- The intervention occurs at the natural pause point (checkout), not any time before.

- Users can choose the pillars (space, need, money) and customize prompts that way, shuffle prompts, and always proceed to checkout if they wish.

- All reflections stay local. Nothing is tracked, saved, or sent anywhere. (Unless they choose to keep a log of their reflections to view later.)

- Playful and tactile, the cards should make reflection feel like an activity, not a chore.

### Brand Design

- Because Sift is a grounded and reflective experience, I chose to use muted colors in my design, with terracotta as the primary color for a pop of color. I wanted the pillars to have their own colors too.

- I named my tool "sift" after deciding to commit to the card-like feel as you sift through decisions, cards, etc., so you don't have to sift through your closet.

- I chose simple typefaces for now but wish to experiment and make the branding more playful as I develop this concept further.

![[Pasted image 20260417210426.png]]

  

---


### User Flow & Designs

>*Please note that none of the designs here are the final designs; visuals, flow, and design decisions may change as testers provide feedback. (Ongoing)*

#### One-Time Onboarding

When the user first visits a shopping website after installing Sift, a clean onboarding overlay appears. The user selects which pillar(s) they want active (Money, Space, or Need). This overlay appears only once during setup; pillar selections are saved persistently but can be easily changed later as the activity progresses.

![[Screenshot 2026-04-17 at 9.05.50 PM.png]]

#### Uninterrupted Shopping

After onboarding, Sift is completely invisible. No badges, no nudges, nothing. The user shops freely.
#### Checkout Interception

When the user clicks "Continue to checkout," Sift intercepts the navigation, hijacks the button, and the card deck appears based on the chosen pillars.

![[Screenshot 2026-04-17 at 9.07.22 PM.png]]

#### The Card Experience

The card experience is the heart of Sift. It features:

- In a Solitaire-style card stack, cards are slightly offset so the edges of the cards behind are visible, creating a tactile, physical feeling.

- The top card displays a prompt question from the user's selected pillars, with a text input field for typed reflection.

- The cards are draggable and snap to the next/previous card.

- Pillar selections on the fly, changes trigger a full card reshuffle.

- An easy out as well, keeping in mind that a shopper may not need the intervention in edge cases like buying gifts for others, etc.

![[Screenshot 2026-04-17 at 9.07.58 PM.png|313]]


>Sample cards from each pillar: 

![[Pasted image 20260417210833.png]]


#### Exit Flow
The goal is a parting message that empowers the shopper to consider their space, money, and needs, encouraging them to enjoy their purchase on their own terms.

(content & designs are currently a work in progress)

## Technical Implementation

**Technology:** Chrome Extension using Manifest V3, built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.  
**Development Workflow:** Development is being conducted using Claude Code, an agentic terminal-based coding tool. The design implementation used is the Figma MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, which translates my Figma designs directly into code.

## Success Criteria

### Design Quality

- Cohesive brand language and visuals

- Logical and kind content design that reasons with shoppers, never guilts them

- Playful, tactile interactions that make reflection feel fun and immersive

### Validation Goals

- Functioning web extension that can be tested with real users to gather feedback

- Evidence that the intervention creates a genuine moment of reflection without frustrating users

- Qualitative feedback indicating users felt supported
